claim: Numerous studies have identified traveling waves in the cortex.
source: Numerous studies have identified traveling waves in the cortex and suggested they play important roles in brain processing.
evidence: This is a general statement about the literature that is supported by citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: Traveling waves are suggested to play important roles in brain processing.
source: Numerous studies have identified traveling waves in the cortex and suggested they play important roles in brain processing.
evidence: This statement references existing literature suggesting functional roles of waves.

claim: Traveling waves are most often measured using macroscopic methods that are unable to assess the local spiking activity underlying wave dynamics.
source: These waves are most often measured using macroscopic methods that are unable to assess the local spiking activity underlying wave dynamics.
evidence: This is supported by discussion of measurement techniques in the introduction and methods sections.

claim: Sequentially activating two discrete brain areas can appear as traveling waves in EEG simulations.
source: We first show that sequentially activating two discrete brain areas can appear as traveling waves in EEG simulations.
evidence: This is directly demonstrated in Figure 1 with EEG simulations.

claim: An analytical model of two sequentially activated regions can generate wave-like activity with variable directions, velocities, and spatial patterns.
source: Using this model, we were able to generate wave-like activity with variable directions, velocities, and spatial patterns, and to map the discriminability limits between traveling waves and modular sequential activations.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3 with analytical modeling results.

claim: Field potentials in turtle cortex ex vivo exhibit wave-like dynamics.
source: We found that while field potentials exhibit wave-like dynamics, the underlying spiking activity was better described by consecutively activated spatially adjacent groups of neurons.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2 with MEA recordings from turtle cortex.

claim: The underlying spiking activity in turtle cortex is better described by consecutively activated spatially adjacent groups of neurons rather than continuously propagating wavefronts.
source: We found that while field potentials exhibit wave-like dynamics, the underlying spiking activity was better described by consecutively activated spatially adjacent groups of neurons.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2 comparing LFP and spiking patterns.

claim: Traveling waves are considered a ubiquitous feature of cortical dynamics.
source: Cortical traveling waves are considered a ubiquitous feature of cortical dynamics and are suggested to play important roles in cortical processing (Muller et al., 2018; Muller and Destexhe, 2012; Sato et al., 2012; Wu, 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to the literature.

claim: Traveling waves are observed across a wide range of spatial and temporal scales.
source: These waves are observed across a wide range of spatial and temporal scales and exhibit a wide repertoire of propagation patterns.
evidence: This is supported by the subsequent detailed examples in the introduction.

claim: Traveling waves can propagate as plane waves.
source: Traveling waves can propagate to specific directions (plane wave) (Lubenov and Siapas, 2009; Massimini et al., 2004; Senseman, 1999; Xu et al., 2007), outward from a center locus (radial waves) (Muller et al., 2014) or rotate around a phase singularity (spiral waves) (Huang et al., 2010; Muller et al., 2016; Prechtl et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies showing plane wave propagation.

claim: Traveling waves can propagate as radial waves outward from a center locus.
source: Traveling waves can propagate to specific directions (plane wave) (Lubenov and Siapas, 2009; Massimini et al., 2004; Senseman, 1999; Xu et al., 2007), outward from a center locus (radial waves) (Muller et al., 2014) or rotate around a phase singularity (spiral waves) (Huang et al., 2010; Muller et al., 2016; Prechtl et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Muller et al., 2014.

claim: Traveling waves can rotate around a phase singularity as spiral waves.
source: Traveling waves can propagate to specific directions (plane wave) (Lubenov and Siapas, 2009; Massimini et al., 2004; Senseman, 1999; Xu et al., 2007), outward from a center locus (radial waves) (Muller et al., 2014) or rotate around a phase singularity (spiral waves) (Huang et al., 2010; Muller et al., 2016; Prechtl et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies showing spiral wave patterns.

claim: Mesoscale waves span a single cortical area.
source: Waves also range in their spatial extent from mesoscale waves spanning a single cortical area (Ferezou et al., 2006; Jancke et al., 2004; Lubenov and Siapas, 2009; Petersen et al., 2003; Reimer et al., 2011; Rubino et al., 2006; Takahashi et al., 2015; Xu et al., 2007), to macroscale waves propagating through multiple brain areas and even across the two hemispheres (Alexander et al., 2013; Goldman et al., 1949; Massimini et al., 2004; Muller et al., 2016; Patten et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to studies of mesoscale waves.

claim: Macroscale waves propagate through multiple brain areas and even across the two hemispheres.
source: Waves also range in their spatial extent from mesoscale waves spanning a single cortical area (Ferezou et al., 2006; Jancke et al., 2004; Lubenov and Siapas, 2009; Petersen et al., 2003; Reimer et al., 2011; Rubino et al., 2006; Takahashi et al., 2015; Xu et al., 2007), to macroscale waves propagating through multiple brain areas and even across the two hemispheres (Alexander et al., 2013; Goldman et al., 1949; Massimini et al., 2004; Muller et al., 2016; Patten et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to studies of macroscale waves.

claim: Cortical waves are characterized by different propagation velocities ranging from millimeters to meters per second.
source: Finally, cortical waves are characterized by different propagation velocities (from millimeters to meters per second) and frequency bands.
evidence: This is supported by the subsequent examples of different wave types.

claim: α-band oscillations (8–12 Hz) travel from occipital to frontal areas.
source: For example, α-band oscillations (8–12 Hz) travel from occipital to frontal areas (Hughes, 1995); γ-band (30–80 Hz) auditory-induced oscillations travel from anterior to posterior (Ribary et al., 1991); and slow wave oscillations (0.1–1 Hz), occurring during sleep, travel from anterior to posterior cortical regions (Massimini et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hughes, 1995.

claim: γ-band (30–80 Hz) auditory-induced oscillations travel from anterior to posterior.
source: For example, α-band oscillations (8–12 Hz) travel from occipital to frontal areas (Hughes, 1995); γ-band (30–80 Hz) auditory-induced oscillations travel from anterior to posterior (Ribary et al., 1991); and slow wave oscillations (0.1–1 Hz), occurring during sleep, travel from anterior to posterior cortical regions (Massimini et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ribary et al., 1991.

claim: Slow wave oscillations (0.1–1 Hz) occurring during sleep travel from anterior to posterior cortical regions.
source: For example, α-band oscillations (8–12 Hz) travel from occipital to frontal areas (Hughes, 1995); γ-band (30–80 Hz) auditory-induced oscillations travel from anterior to posterior (Ribary et al., 1991); and slow wave oscillations (0.1–1 Hz), occurring during sleep, travel from anterior to posterior cortical regions (Massimini et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Massimini et al., 2004.

claim: The cortex has modular structural and functional organization.
source: It is unclear how the abundance of traveling waves across large areas of cortex fits its modular structural and functional organization (Meunier et al., 2010; Sporns and Betzel, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on cortical modularity.

claim: Tangential cortical connectivity is not uniform.
source: Tangential cortical connectivity is not uniform.
evidence: This is supported by the subsequent examples of connectivity differences.

claim: Tangential cortical connectivity is higher within cortical areas than between areas.
source: It is higher within cortical areas (e.g. V1) or regions (e.g. visual cortex) than between areas (V1 and V2 or visual cortex and auditory cortex) (Harris et al., 2019; Hilgetag et al., 2000; Jia et al., 2022; Markov et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to connectivity studies.

claim: Cortical modularity is observed across multiple scales.
source: This modularity is observed across multiple scales.
evidence: This is supported by the subsequent example of columnar organization.

claim: Within single cortical areas, neurons are segmented into columns with high intra-column connectivity and sparser inter-column connectivity.
source: Within single cortical areas, neurons are segmented into columns with high intra-column connectivity and sparser inter-column connectivity (Mountcastle, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mountcastle, 1997.

claim: Non-uniform connectivity is likely to restrict the spread of activity rather than support smooth propagation of waves across the cortical sheet.
source: Such non-uniform connectivity is likely to restrict the spread of activity rather than to support smooth propagation of waves across the cortical sheet during which action potentials are sequentially activated in neurons as the wavefront passes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural properties of cortical connectivity.

claim: One of the roles of modularity is to segregate circuits and computation.
source: Indeed, it was suggested that one of the roles of modularity is to segregate circuits and computation (Jia et al., 2022; Shein-Idelson et al., 2016) and prevent uncontrolled spread of excitability, as is evident in pathological conditions such as epileptic seizures (Martinet et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on modularity function.

claim: Modularity prevents uncontrolled spread of excitability, as is evident in pathological conditions such as epileptic seizures.
source: Indeed, it was suggested that one of the roles of modularity is to segregate circuits and computation (Jia et al., 2022; Shein-Idelson et al., 2016) and prevent uncontrolled spread of excitability, as is evident in pathological conditions such as epileptic seizures (Martinet et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Martinet et al., 2017 on epileptic seizures.

claim: Determining whether a traveling wave entails a spreading excitation at the single neuron level requires single cell resolution measurements.
source: For example, determining whether a traveling wave entails a spreading excitation at the single neuron level requires single cell resolution measurements.
evidence: This is a logical inference about measurement requirements.

claim: Traveling waves are commonly measured with low spatial resolution techniques.
source: In contrast, traveling waves are commonly measured with low spatial resolution technique (Hindriks et al., 2014; Mak-McCully et al., 2015; Muller et al., 2016; Ribary et al., 1991).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies using low-resolution techniques.

claim: In EEG, brain current sources are distant from the measurement electrodes and separated by diffracting elements such as the skull.
source: This is especially true for extracranial recording such as EEG in which brain current sources are distant from the measurement electrodes and separated by diffracting elements such as the skull (Michel and Murray, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Michel and Murray, 2012 and is established knowledge about EEG.

claim: In ECoG, volume conduction through low impedance media such as cerebrospinal fluid may result in substantial contribution of distant areas to local measurements.
source: Even in more local intracranial measurements such as electrocorticography (ECoG), volume conduction through low impedance media, such as the cerebrospinal fluid, may result in substantial contribution of distant areas to local measurements and effective spatial low-pass filtering that blur out possible spatially segregated activations (Buzsáki et al., 2012; Herreras, 2016; Kajikawa and Schroeder, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on volume conduction effects.

claim: VSD measurements mostly reflect sub-threshold potentials.
source: While the spatial resolution of this method is higher, VSD measurements mostly reflect sub-threshold potentials (Chemla and Chavane, 2010a) with strong contribution from upper layers and long-range inputs (Chemla and Chavane, 2010b; Petersen et al., 2003; Stepanyants et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chemla and Chavane, 2010a.

claim: VSD measurements have strong contribution from upper layers and long-range inputs.
source: While the spatial resolution of this method is higher, VSD measurements mostly reflect sub-threshold potentials (Chemla and Chavane, 2010a) with strong contribution from upper layers and long-range inputs (Chemla and Chavane, 2010b; Petersen et al., 2003; Stepanyants et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on VSD signal sources.

claim: VSDs integrate inputs from both local and distant spiking activities rather than represent local spiking excitability profiles.
source: Thus, VSDs integrate inputs from both local and distant spiking activities rather than represent local spiking excitability profiles.
evidence: This is an inference based on the properties of VSD measurements described.

claim: VSD signals may be contaminated by contribution from non-neuronal sources.
source: In addition, VSD signals may be contaminated by contribution from non-neuronal sources (Pál et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pál et al., 2015.

claim: The velocities of some traveling waves correspond to axonal propagation.
source: For example, the velocities of some traveling waves correspond to axonal propagation (Muller and Destexhe, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Muller and Destexhe, 2012.

claim: Axonal propagations do not necessarily activate the neurons in the target tissue and single cell excitability may remain modular.
source: However, such axonal propagations do not necessarily activate the neurons in the target tissue and single cell excitability may remain modular.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the relationship between axonal propagation and neuronal activation.

claim: In specific cases the existence of traveling waves in single cells was measured in high resolution.
source: While in specific cases the existence of traveling waves in single cells was measured in high resolution (Lubenov and Siapas, 2009; Voufo et al., 2023), this existence cannot be unambiguously generalized to all reported traveling waves, especially given the large diversity of reported wave patterns across different brain areas.
evidence: This is supported by citations to specific studies showing single-cell waves.

claim: The existence of single-cell traveling waves cannot be unambiguously generalized to all reported traveling waves.
source: While in specific cases the existence of traveling waves in single cells was measured in high resolution (Lubenov and Siapas, 2009; Voufo et al., 2023), this existence cannot be unambiguously generalized to all reported traveling waves, especially given the large diversity of reported wave patterns across different brain areas.
evidence: This is an inference based on the diversity of wave patterns and limited single-cell measurements.

claim: Previous studies raised the possibility that measured propagating patterns may be biased by the limitations of experimental technique used.
source: In addition to the lack of understanding of the nature of excitability underlying waves, previous studies raised the possibility that measured propagating patterns may be biased by the limitations of experimental technique used (Muller et al., 2014; Wu, 2008; Zhigalov and Jensen, 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies discussing methodological limitations.

claim: A stationary source with a spatially decaying profile that increases over time can result in a false measurement of a propagating wave.
source: For example, when considering a scenario in which the intensity of a stationary source with a spatially decaying profile increases over time. In this scenario, additional regions cross the detection threshold at progressively longer times and may result in a false measurement of a propagating wave.
evidence: This is a logical inference about how measurement artifacts can arise.

claim: The phase latency map (PLM) allows discrimination between a stationary bump and a traveling wave.
source: To address this caveat, Muller et al. introduced the phase latency map (PLM) allowing them to discriminate between a stationary bump and a traveling wave and to conclude that propagating waves were measured (Muller et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Muller et al., 2014.

claim: A mixture of stationary sources can result in wave-like patterns in EEG recordings.
source: For example, it was recently shown that a mixture of stationary sources can result in WLPs in EEG recordings (Zhigalov and Jensen, 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zhigalov and Jensen, 2023.

claim: Current source density reveals wave-like patterns following sequential activation of different cortical lamina.
source: Similarly, current source density reveals WLPs following sequential activation of different cortical lamina (Orczyk et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Orczyk et al., 2021.

claim: The criteria for differentiating wave-like patterns from traveling waves remains unknown.
source: Despite these concerns, the criteria for differentiating WLPs from traveling waves remains unknown.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in current knowledge.

claim: Evidence for the existence of wave-like patterns on the single neuron level is missing.
source: Further, evidence for the existence of WLPs on the single neuron level is missing.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in current knowledge.

claim: Two brain areas defined on the cortex by sets of dipoles were activated uniformly with a time delay between areas in the EEG simulation.
source: Two brain areas (green and red ellipses) are defined on the cortex by a set of dipoles that are activated uniformly with a time delay (ΔT) between areas.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1A and described in the methods.

claim: A continuous delay pattern propagating from posterior to anterior was observed in the EEG simulation with two sequentially activated dipole sets.
source: Latency to peak measured across electrodes following the sequential activation of two sets of dipoles (green and red circles in the background) with a distance of 11 cm (Δx/σx=16.9) and time delay of 20 ms (ΔT/σT=0.2). A continuous delay pattern propagating from posterior (P) to anterior (A) is observed.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B.

claim: PLDC remains close to 1 (indicating apparent wave propagation) for a wide range of distance and delay values in the EEG simulation.
source: Phase latency distance correlations (PLDCs) for different distances and different delays between two activated areas. PLDC remains close to 1 (indicating apparent wave propagation) for a wide range of values.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Filtering increases PLDC values making them more wave-like in the EEG simulation.
source: Filtering increases PLDC values making rendering them more wave-like.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Visual stimulation elicited increases in LFPs and spikes across large regions of the visual cortex in turtle.
source: Corresponding with previous reports (Prechtl et al., 2000), visual stimulation elicited increases in LFPs and spikes (Figure 2B – gray and black traces respectively) across large regions of the visual cortex.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B and supported by citation.

claim: Responses to visual stimulation in turtle cortex typically started ~200 ms post-stimulus and lasted for ~2 s.
source: Although responses varied in intensity between stimulations, they typically started ~200 ms post-stimulus and lasted for ~2 s.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the experimental data.

claim: Responses to visual stimulation in turtle cortex were characterized by high power at low frequencies.
source: Spectral analysis revealed that responses were characterized by high power at low frequencies (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C with spectral analysis.

claim: Averaging over all trials revealed a clear propagation pattern traveling from anterolateral to posteromedial in turtle cortex.
source: Averaging over all trials revealed a clear propagation pattern traveling from anterolateral to posteromedial (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The propagation pattern in turtle cortex was consistent with previous reports of waves traveling from area D2 to area D1.
source: This pattern was consistent with previous reports of waves traveling from area D2 to area D1 in turtle cortex (Prechtl et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Prechtl et al., 1997.

claim: The maximum of the first oscillation cycle showed a clear propagation pattern with a velocity of 1.8±0.35 mm/s in turtle cortex.
source: The maximum showed a clear propagation pattern with a velocity of 1.8±0.35 mm/s (mean ± sd).
evidence: This is calculated from the data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: PLDC values for the first oscillation cycle in response to visual stimulation were close to 1 suggesting the existence of propagating waves in turtle cortex.
source: We next calculated the PLDC values for the first oscillation cycle in response to visual stimulation across all trials and plotted their distribution (Figure 2F – blue). PLDC values were close to 1 suggesting the existence of propagating waves.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Shuffling the channels' phase latencies dramatically reduced PLDC to an average close to zero in turtle cortex data.
source: For comparison, calculating PLDC after shuffling the channels' phase latencies dramatically reduced PLDC to an average close to zero (Figure 2F – red).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2F as a control analysis.

claim: Spikes were generally locked to the LFP oscillation with a peak spiking rate at a phase of 0.53π in turtle cortex.
source: Spikes were generally locked to the LFP oscillation with a peak spiking rate at a phase of 0.53π (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A.

claim: LFP phase crossings were temporally continuous and did not strongly deviate from a uniform distribution in turtle cortex.
source: The LFP phase crossings were temporally continuous and therefore did not strongly deviate from a uniform distribution (Figure 2H – top, p-value 0.85).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2H with DIP test results.

claim: Spike timings were segregated into temporal groups and were not unimodally distributed in turtle cortex.
source: In contrast, spike timings were segregated into temporal groups and were not unimodally distributed (Figure 2H – bottom, p-value <0.0002).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2H with DIP test results.

claim: The DIP test showed consistently larger values for spikes vs. LFP across trials in turtle cortex.
source: The results showed a consistently larger DIP for spikes vs. LFP (Figure 2K – red vs blue areas).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2K.

claim: The difference in DIP values between spikes and LFP was significant when comparing pairwise differences calculated for each trial separately in turtle cortex.
source: This difference was not only significant on the average level but was also evident when comparing the p-value of pairwise differences calculated for each trial separately (Figure 2K – gray area).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2K.

claim: The difference between LFP and spiking patterns was consistent across recordings in other animals.
source: Finally, repeating this analysis for recordings in other animals reveals consistent results (Figure 2M), indicating that while LFP activity along the wave path resembles a continuously propagating wave, the spiking activity – a marker of local excitability – is more consistent with sequentially activated spatially segregated modules.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2M across multiple experiments.

claim: The ALSA phase distribution resembled that obtained with single spikes but was more sharply locked to the LFP oscillation phase in turtle cortex.
source: Correspondingly, the ALSA phase distribution resembled that obtained with single spikes but was more sharply locked to the LFP oscillation phase (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3B.

claim: The ALSA onset times did not evolve continuously across space but were organized in two separate and sequentially activated spatial groups in turtle cortex.
source: In contrast to the LFP (Figure 2I, Figure 2—figure supplement 4A–C), the ALSA onset times did not evolve continuously across space but were organized in two separate and sequentially activated spatial groups (Figure 2J, Figure 2—figure supplement 4D–F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2J and Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: Comparing the DIP test for LFP and ALSA revealed a consistent difference across trials in both the average DIP values and the difference in single trials in turtle cortex.
source: Comparing the DIP test for LFP and ALSA revealed a consistent difference across trials in both the average DIP values and the difference in single trials (Figure 2L) that replicated over experiments (Figure 2N).
evidence: This is shown in Figures 2L and 2N.

claim: Propagating patterns were detected in other frequency bands including 12–35 Hz in turtle cortex.
source: We note that we focused the above analysis on waves in the low-frequency LFP band (0–2 Hz) because these events recruited enough spikes to analyze their phase relations. However, propagating patterns were also detected in other frequency bands (Figure 2—figure supplement 5) and showed complex patterns including plane waves, radial waves, and spiral waves.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5.

claim: For Δx≤2σx the spatial profile of two sequentially activated Gaussians is concave.
source: Notice that for Δx≤2σx the spatial profile is concave.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3B and derived analytically in Appendix 1.

claim: The average velocity of the propagating peak increases with the distance between Gaussian centers (Δx).
source: Notice that the average velocity increases with Δx.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Wave velocity increases with frequency in the periodic Gaussian model.
source: Notice that wave velocity increases with frequency and can change sign as a function of Δϕ.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3H and derived from Equation 4.

claim: Wave velocity can change sign as a function of the phase difference between Gaussians (Δϕ).
source: Notice that wave velocity increases with frequency and can change sign as a function of Δϕ.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3G and derived from Equation 4.

claim: Using a combination of only two sequentially activated Gaussians, a wide range of phase latency profiles corresponding to plane, radial, and spiral-like waves could be generated.
source: These examples illustrate that using a combination of only two sequentially activated Gaussians, a wide range of phase latency profiles corresponding to plane, radial, and spiral-like waves could be generated.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3J.

claim: LFP measurements indicative of waves propagating across turtle cortex are underlined by discrete and consecutively activated neuronal populations.
source: We showed that LFP measurements indicative of waves propagating across turtle cortex are underlined by discrete and consecutively activated neuronal populations, and not by a continuously propagating wavefront of spikes (Figure 2).
evidence: This is the main finding demonstrated in Figure 2.

claim: Activation profiles that resemble continuous traveling waves in EEG simulations can be underlined by consecutive activation of two discrete cortical regions.
source: Similarly, activation profiles that resemble continuous traveling waves in EEG simulations can be underlined by consecutive activation of two discrete cortical regions (Figure 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 1.

claim: A simple scenario of sequentially activated Gaussians can exhibit wave-like patterns with a rich diversity of spatiotemporal profiles.
source: We replicated these results using an analytical model and demonstrated that a simple scenario of sequentially activated Gaussians can exhibit WLPs with a rich diversity of spatiotemporal profiles (Figure 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3.

claim: The main parameter affecting the detection of wave-like patterns in a sequentially activated modular system is the distance between modules relative to their spatial spread.
source: Our analytical results suggest that the main parameter affecting the detection of WLPs in a sequentially activated modular system is the distance between modules relative to their spatial spread.
evidence: This is derived from the analytical model in Figure 3 and Appendix 1.

claim: The spatial spread in potential-based measurements will markedly increase with medium conductance and distance from the source.
source: For potential-based measurements, the spread will markedly increase with medium conductance and distance from the source, as predicted from the volume conductance theory (Buzsáki et al., 2012).
evidence: This is based on volume conduction theory cited from Buzsáki et al., 2012.

claim: Spatial spread will be large in EEG measurements where the distance between the sources and the electrodes is large.
source: Our simulations show that spatial spread will be large in EEG measurements (Figure 1) where the distance between the sources and the electrodes is large, and the skull and meninges disperse the electrical field generated by localized cortical currents (Akalin Acar et al., 2016; Kajikawa and Schroeder, 2011).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 1 and supported by citations.

claim: Dispersion can be substantial in intracranial measurements such as ECoG due to the high conductivity of the cerebrospinal fluid.
source: Dispersion can also be substantial in intracranial measurements such as ECoG due to the high conductivity of the cerebrospinal fluid (Buzsáki et al., 2012; Herreras, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on volume conduction.

claim: Large spread was observed in MEA LFP recordings from turtle cortex despite small distance between tissue and electrodes.
source: Interestingly, large spread was also observed in our MEA LFP recordings, where no meninges separate between the electrodes and tissue. Further, the small distance between the tissue and the electrodes limits conductance through the artificial cerebrospinal fluid. Despite this, propagation appeared spatially continuous in LFP, suggesting contributions from volume conduction through the tissue and non-local current sources, for example, activated synaptic terminals from axons of distant neurons.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results in Figure 2.

claim: Theoretical studies calculate spatial decay constants of hundreds of micrometers for LFP.
source: This spread is aligned with theoretical studies calculating spatial decay constants of hundreds of micrometers (Lindén et al., 2010) and with experiments reporting contributions from sources millimeters away (Kajikawa and Schroeder, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lindén et al., 2010.

claim: Experiments report LFP contributions from sources millimeters away.
source: This spread is aligned with theoretical studies calculating spatial decay constants of hundreds of micrometers (Lindén et al., 2010) and with experiments reporting contributions from sources millimeters away (Kajikawa and Schroeder, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kajikawa and Schroeder, 2011.

claim: Light scatters in optical signals, especially in wide-field imaging.
source: However, light scatters in optical signals, especially in wide-field imaging.
evidence: This is established knowledge about optical imaging.

claim: VSD measurements report subthreshold potentials integrating excitability from large areas due to synaptic currents originating from long-distance neurons in addition to local ones.
source: More importantly, VSD measurements report subthreshold potentials integrating excitability from large areas due to synaptic currents originating from long-distance neurons in addition to local ones (Chemla and Chavane, 2010a; Petersen et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on VSD signal sources.

claim: Deflection of a single whisker results in cortical activation that extends beyond the corresponding barrel.
source: Correspondingly, deflection of a single whisker results in cortical activation that extends beyond the corresponding barrel (Ferezou et al., 2006; Petersen et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: Averaging may smooth the boundaries between modules in combination with the inherent variability in neuronal signals.
source: In combination with the inherent variability in neuronal signals (Fox et al., 2006), averaging may smooth the boundaries between modules (Mouraux and Iannetti, 2008), effectively increase the spatial spread, and therefore promote the identification of WLPs.
evidence: This is supported by citations and is a logical inference about averaging effects.

claim: Averaging may explain the smoother LFP profiles after averaging relative to single trials in turtle cortex.
source: Such a spread may explain the smoother LFP profiles after averaging (Figure 2D) relative to single trials (Figure 2G, I) in turtle cortex.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing averaged and single trial data in Figure 2.

claim: Discriminability between Gaussian activations will decrease with increase in σt.
source: Thus, discriminability between Gaussian activations will decrease with increase in σt, for example, following filtering.
evidence: This is inferred from the analytical model results.

claim: Filtering into narrow frequency bands is a common practice in EEG research and is liable to smoothen sharp transients.
source: Indeed, filtering into narrow frequency bands is a common practice in EEG research and is liable to smoothen sharp transients.
evidence: This is established knowledge about signal processing effects.

claim: Filtering markedly increased PLDC by effectively smoothing the activation boundaries between modules in EEG simulations.
source: Correspondingly, our EEG simulations indicate that filtering markedly increased PLDC by effectively smoothing the activation boundaries between modules (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: PLMs and PLDC analysis are valuable steps toward differentiating between single stationary bumps and traveling waves.
source: PLMs and PLDC analysis are valuable steps toward differentiating between single stationary bumps and traveling waves (Muller et al., 2014) and continue to be used to date (Davis et al., 2020; Muller et al., 2018; Muller et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies using these methods.

claim: The underlying assumption behind PLM/PLDC is that a stationary bump is characterized by a flat latency map.
source: The underlying assumption behind this approach is that a stationary bump is characterized by a flat latency map because every channel reaches its maximum at the same time, rather than the latency increasing in a particular direction, in case of a wave.
evidence: This is an explanation of the logic behind the PLM method.

claim: The PLM/PLDC approach does not consider the possibility of sequentially activated local populations.
source: However, this approach does not consider the possibility of sequentially activated local populations.
evidence: This is a critique based on the results of this study.

claim: Activity profiles resulting from two sequentially activated Gaussians meet the phase latency conditions for waves.
source: Indeed, our results show how activity profiles resulting from two sequentially activated Gaussians meet the phase latency conditions for waves.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figures 1 and 3.

claim: The propagation direction of wave-like patterns is determined by the location of sequentially activated modules.
source: We showed that the propagation direction of WLPs is determined by the location of sequentially activated modules (Figure 1) and the propagation speed of WLPs by the distance between modules and their temporal delay (Figure 3, Equation 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figures 1 and 3.

claim: The propagation speed of wave-like patterns is determined by the distance between modules and their temporal delay.
source: We showed that the propagation direction of WLPs is determined by the location of sequentially activated modules (Figure 1) and the propagation speed of WLPs by the distance between modules and their temporal delay (Figure 3, Equation 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3 and Equation 2.

claim: When calculating propagation speeds for narrow-band signals, velocities increase with frequency band.
source: In addition, when calculating propagation speeds for narrow-band signals, velocities increase with frequency band and may even reverse direction as a function of the phase lag between oscillatory areas (Equation 4 and Figure 3G–H).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3G-H and Equation 4.

claim: Propagation direction may reverse as a function of the phase lag between oscillatory areas.
source: In addition, when calculating propagation speeds for narrow-band signals, velocities increase with frequency band and may even reverse direction as a function of the phase lag between oscillatory areas (Equation 4 and Figure 3G–H).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3G and Equation 4.

claim: Cortical waves in the same tissue can propagate both in forward and backward directions.
source: These results are interesting given that cortical waves in the same tissue can propagate both in forward and backward directions and that higher frequencies propagate faster (Bahramisharif et al., 2013; Halgren et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: Higher frequencies propagate faster in cortical waves.
source: These results are interesting given that cortical waves in the same tissue can propagate both in forward and backward directions and that higher frequencies propagate faster (Bahramisharif et al., 2013; Halgren et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: Cortical responses to similar stimuli vary in propagation profile for EEG and MEG recordings.
source: The above results echo findings in a recent study showing that cortical responses to similar stimuli vary in propagation profile for EEG and MEG recordings and that this discrepancy can be accounted by modeling sequentially activated sources (Lozano-Soldevilla and VanRullen, 2019; Zhigalov and Jensen, 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent studies.

claim: Several reports suggest that waves are underlined by propagation along axonal collaterals.
source: Several reports suggest that waves are underlined by propagation along axonal collaterals (Muller et al., 2018; Muller et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on wave mechanisms.

claim: Axonal waves travel at high propagation speeds and are not compatible with the wide diversity of wave velocities.
source: However, such waves travel at high propagation speeds and are not compatible with the wide diversity of wave velocities and mechanisms of local neuronal interactions (Ermentrout and Kleinfeld, 2001; Feller et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citations and is a logical inference.

claim: The temporal grouping of spike timings across two regions of turtle cortex is spatially aligned with a structural transition between areas D1 and D2.
source: While modularity in turtle cortex connectivity structure was not systematically mapped, the temporal grouping of spike timings across two regions of turtle cortex (Figure 2J) is spatially aligned with a structural transition between areas D1 and D2 (Desan, 1984; Prechtl et al., 1997).
evidence: This is inferred from the data in Figure 2J and supported by citations.

claim: The structural transition between D1 and D2 was not evident in the LFPs in turtle cortex.
source: This transition was not evident in the LFPs, possibly due to the longer decay constants of slow potentials and the existing connection between D2 and D1.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results in Figure 2.

claim: Measurements from retinas ex vivo were performed across large areas with single cell resolution using both calcium imaging and dense electrode arrays.
source: Measurements from retinas ex vivo were performed across large areas with single cell resolution using both calcium imaging and dense electrode arrays (Ackman et al., 2012; Newman and Zahs, 1997; Voufo et al., 2023; Zheng et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on retinal waves.

claim: In retinal measurements, spatially adjacent neurons were shown to be activated sequentially in two-dimensional spreading patterns.
source: In such measurements, spatially adjacent neurons were shown to be activated sequentially in two-dimensional spreading patterns.
evidence: This is supported by the cited retinal wave studies.

claim: Traveling waves were detected in developing cortex, thalamus, and other brain areas.
source: Traveling waves were also detected in developing cortex, thalamus, and other brain areas (Ackman et al., 2012; Hanganu et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to developmental studies.

claim: In mature circuits, connectivity and excitability profiles are replaced by modules and by segregated excitability.
source: In contrast, in mature circuits, and specifically in cortex, connectivity and possibly excitability profiles are replaced by modules and by segregated excitability (Chen et al., 2008; Kaiser and Hilgetag, 2010; Meunier et al., 2010; Mountcastle, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on cortical organization.

claim: Traveling waves may dominate in specific conditions of reduced consciousness such as anesthesia or sleep.
source: Accordingly, traveling waves may dominate in specific conditions of reduced consciousness such as anesthesia or sleep (Liang et al., 2023; Liang et al., 2021; Massimini et al., 2004; Muller et al., 2018; Xu et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on waves during altered states.

claim: Waves are reported under pathological conditions such as epilepsy.
source: Interestingly, waves are also reported under pathological conditions such as epilepsy (van den Berg et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a study on epileptic waves.

claim: In epilepsy, inhibition in the network is reduced which may lead to replacement of modular segregated activation by large-scale propagation of excitability.
source: In such states, inhibition in the network is reduced (Sloviter, 1987) which may lead to a replacement of modular segregated activation by large-scale propagation of excitability crossing modular boundaries (Shein-Idelson et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations and is a logical inference about network dynamics.

claim: Wave propagation patterns on the single cell level are only scarcely reported during wakefulness.
source: Indeed, wave propagation patterns on the single cell level are only scarcely reported during wakefulness (Davis et al., 2020; Lubenov and Siapas, 2009) leaving the microscopic correlates of most traveling wave unknown.
evidence: This is supported by limited citations to single-cell wave studies during wakefulness.

claim: Calcium imaging data supports both localized sequential activations and traveling motifs.
source: The data provided by this method supports both localized sequential activations (Nietz et al., 2023) and traveling motifs (Afrashteh et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to calcium imaging studies.

claim: No analysis was performed to discriminate between waves and sequentially activated sources and sinks in calcium imaging studies.
source: However, to the best of our knowledge, no analysis was performed to discriminate between waves and sequentially activated sources and sinks.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in the calcium imaging literature.

claim: The temporal resolution of calcium imaging is low, making it hard to detect temporal boundaries, especially for fast oscillating waves.
source: In addition, the temporal resolution of calcium imaging is low, making it hard to detect temporal boundaries, especially for fast oscillating waves (e.g. in the γ-range).
evidence: This is established knowledge about calcium imaging limitations.

claim: Wide point spread functions, axonal projections, or sparse activation of adjacent populations may mask circuit modularity and promote wave detection in calcium imaging.
source: Further, wide point spread functions, axonal projections, or sparse activation of adjacent populations may mask circuit modularity and promote wave detection (Ali and Kwan, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation and is a logical inference about imaging artifacts.

claim: The ex vivo eye-brain turtle preparation allows large-scale two-dimensional sampling of both spiking and LFP activity.
source: The advantage of this preparation is that it allows large-scale two-dimensional (in directions tangential to the cortical surface) sampling of both spiking and LFP activity.
evidence: This describes the experimental advantages of the turtle preparation.

claim: Previous works with the turtle preparation have shown the existence of waves that travel across cortex following visual stimulation.
source: Furthermore, previous works with this preparation have shown the existence of waves that travel across cortex following visual stimulation (Prechtl et al., 1997; Senseman and Robbins, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The basic excitability features of turtle cortex and mammalian cortex are similar.
source: Finally, while the layered organization of turtle cortex is different than that of mammalian cortex, the basic excitability features of both tissues are similar (Connors and Kriegstein, 1986; Hemberger et al., 2019; Kriegstein and Connors, 1986; Larkum et al., 2008; Shein-Idelson et al., 2017), and substantial differences in the manner by which field potentials and spikes spread through the tissue are not to be expected.
evidence: This is supported by citations to comparative studies.
